clinicalPearls: Squamous papilloma is one of the commonest benign eyelid lesions, presenting as a skin-coloured, sessile or pedunculated growth, often with a raspberry-like or frond-like surface, frequently along the lid margin.
Lesions may be single or multiple; multiple or filiform verrucous papillomas, especially in children or the immunosuppressed, are often viral (human papillomavirus) in origin.
The diagnosis is usually clinical, but any pigmented, ulcerated, indurated or rapidly changing eyelid lesion should be regarded as suspicious and biopsied.
Involvement of the lid margin and lash line can cause chronic irritation, tear-film disturbance and cosmetic concern; a lesion touching the ocular surface may cause foreign-body sensation.
Small asymptomatic papillomas can simply be observed; symptomatic or cosmetically troublesome ones are treated by shave or complete excision, with cautery or cryotherapy for viral lesions.
Recurrence is more likely with incomplete excision and with viral papillomas, which may also seed adjacent skin.
Loss of eyelashes (madarosis), destruction of the lid margin architecture, or ulceration should prompt suspicion of basal cell or sebaceous carcinoma masquerading as a benign papilloma.
Histology after excision is prudent for any lesion with atypical features, since malignant eyelid tumours can closely mimic a benign papilloma.
reference.pathophysiology: A squamous papilloma is a benign proliferation of the eyelid surface epithelium characterised by acanthosis, hyperkeratosis and papillomatosis over fibrovascular cores. Two overlapping mechanisms operate: chronic actinic and mechanical irritation drives an involutional, non-infective epithelial overgrowth typical of the sessile lesions of older adults, whereas human papillomavirus infection of keratinocytes produces the filiform verrucous lesions, often multiple, seen in younger or immunosuppressed patients. In both, the epithelium folds into finger-like projections supported by vascularised connective-tissue cores, but there is no dermal invasion or cytological malignancy.
additionalDifferentials: Basal cell carcinoma of the eyelid
Squamous cell carcinoma or actinic keratosis
additionalInvestigations: Slit-lamp and external examination to define margins, lash involvement and surface pattern
Dermoscopy to assess vascular and surface features
External and anterior-segment photography for documentation and monitoring
Excisional biopsy with histopathology for atypical, pigmented or recurrent lesions
Assessment of immune status when lesions are multiple or florid
Regional lymph node examination if malignancy is suspected
redFlags: Ulceration, induration, bleeding or a pearly rolled edge suggesting basal cell carcinoma
Loss of eyelashes or destruction of lid-margin architecture suggesting sebaceous or basal cell carcinoma
Rapid growth, irregular pigmentation or asymmetry
Diffuse or chronic unilateral blepharitis mimicking a benign lesion but concealing sebaceous carcinoma
reference.prognosis: Benign with an excellent prognosis; complete excision is generally curative. Viral and incompletely excised lesions may recur, and multiple lesions can persist, but there is no threat to vision or life.
pitfalls: Assuming all verrucous eyelid lesions are benign and missing a malignancy presenting with madarosis or ulceration
Incomplete excision of viral papillomas leading to recurrence and local spread
Cryotherapy or cautery close to the lid margin causing notching, trichiasis or lash loss
Failing to send excised tissue for histology when features are atypical
Overlooking immunosuppression in a patient with multiple or recurrent lesions
references: Kanski's Clinical Ophthalmology: A Systematic Approach
American Academy of Ophthalmology, Basic and Clinical Science Course — Oculofacial Plastic and Orbital Surgery
management: Observe small, asymptomatic lesions, as they are benign and pose no threat to vision
Shave or complete surgical excision for symptomatic, irritating or cosmetically troublesome lesions
Cautery or cryotherapy for viral (human papillomavirus) papillomas
Excisional biopsy with histopathology for any pigmented, ulcerated, indurated or rapidly changing lesion to exclude malignancy
Aim for complete excision to reduce recurrence, which is more likely with incomplete removal or viral lesions
Assess immune status when lesions are multiple or florid and manage any associated lid-margin irritation, referring to ophthalmology
